payload.headline: NVIDIA drops 5.86% to 155.38 as Huang comeback rally fades; still hold

summary.thesis: NVIDIA's cash generation is exceptional, and today's price already assumes free cash flow starts growing at about 20% a year. The upside depends on a record 65% operating margin holding.
summary.decision: Hold the long-term position and make no swing trade while the price sits between support and resistance in a downtrend.
summary.act_at: Buy at 116.97, move to wait on a close below 147.14, trim near 222.58

payload.happening: NVIDIA fell 5.86% to 155.38, giving back part of the rally that followed Jensen Huang's reported return as CEO. Headlines today are mostly about governance: the government's role in his return, open investigations, and a reported addition of Megaspeed to the U.S. trade blacklist over export controls. Our data has no earnings date, and the latest filed quarter ended 2026-07-26.
payload.business: The business numbers are strong. Over the last twelve months revenue was 303.0B, up from 165.2B. Free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) was 127.0B, up from 72.0B. Operating margin rose to 65.21% from 58.09%, and the company holds 23.2B more cash than debt. None of today's CEO news changes these figures. The leadership drama, the investigations and Huang reportedly saying he still does not believe in succession planning affect sentiment and governance, not demand. Two items could touch the business. First, the Megaspeed blacklisting (reported) concerns export controls, which can limit where chips are sold (general knowledge). Second, Amazon's reported Decart deal is a bet on narrowing the chip gap with NVIDIA, a long-run competition risk. The real risks come from the filings. The 65% margin sits at the top of its 5-year range of 16–65%, and peaks like that usually fade. Money customers still owe is up 127% while quarterly sales are up 106%, which can mean sales were pulled forward or customers are stretched. Demand itself does not look at risk today. What is at risk is how long the margin and the payment timing hold.

worth.text: The two methods disagree mainly because they make different assumptions about growth. A discounted cash flow model values the company from its expected future cash. Using the 127.0B in trailing free cash flow and a discount rate near 10%, it gives 191.49 (bear), 222.58 (base) and 264.22 (bull). The company's own price-to-sales history gives 217.35 to 411.04. The more useful reading runs the other way. At 155.38, the price matches the model value of 155.64, which is what 20% starting growth produces, and the data puts the implied starting growth at 20.0%. So the market is not paying for the 83% sales growth of last year. It is paying for growth to slow sharply. The biggest swing factor is margin. If operating margin falls to 48%, the value drops to 116.97, and at 32% it drops to 78.3. The data's valuation summary quotes an older price of 165.05, so today's price sits even lower against those ranges. Multiples tell the same story: 19.6 times trailing earnings, 9.4 times next year's expected earnings, and 12.4 times sales against a peer median of 14.9.
worth.key_assumption: Operating margin stays near 65.21% rather than fading toward 48%, while free cash flow grows from 127.0B at a starting rate of about 20% or more.

bull: The stock trades at 9.4 times analysts' next-year earnings estimate, and that estimate has risen 27.7% over 90 days.
Free cash flow reached 127.0B, up from 72.0B, with 23.2B more cash than debt.
Price-to-sales of 12.4 is below the peer median of 14.9 and sits at the 9th percentile of NVIDIA's own 5-year range.
bear: Operating margin of 65% is at the top of its 5-year range of 16–65%, and a fade to 48% would put model value at 116.97.
Money customers owe is up 127% against sales up 106%, which can be a sign of pulled-forward sales or stretched customers.
The trend is down, and the price sits well below the 50-day average of 204.95 and the falling 20-day average of 175.78.

levels.what: Bottom of the only support zone (147.14–150.46). A close below it moves the call to wait.
Model value if operating margin falls to 48%. Buy at 116.97, because that price already allows for a large margin fade.
Base-case cash-flow value. Trim near it, because at that price the market would be paying for the full current margin and growth.

longterm.why: The automated rule says 'Buy now' and the committee says 'Hold'. The price already assumes about 20% growth and relies on a peak margin, and the slow-payment risk is unresolved, so the call is hold rather than add.

swing.why: The price sits between support at 147.14–150.46 and resistance at 163.9–171.33 (4 touches), in a downtrend. A typical day's range is 13.32, which would blow through a tight stop. No trade until the price holds the 147.14–150.46 zone or closes above 171.33.

decision.timing: Our data has no earnings date. The next quarterly filing will show whether the 65.21% margin and customer payments hold. The options data is from 2026-11-23 and priced off 165.05, so its expected moves are out of date after today's drop.

change_mind: A close below 147.14 would break the only support zone and move the long-term call from hold to wait.
If the next filing shows operating margin falling back toward 58.09%, or the gap between money owed (up 127%) and sales (up 106%) widening, the fair-value view moves toward 116.97.
A close above 171.33, the top of the 4-touch resistance zone, would turn the swing call from wait to enter.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: hold, confirmed by the price falling to 155.38, which matches the 155.64 value implied by 20% starting growth (the margin-fade value at 48% is now 116.97, up from 114.82).
payload.label: Research, not advice.
